questions.q: Per this lesson, why is a quality problem in master data worse than one in a one-off report?
options: Because master data is shared, so a single wrong value flows out to every downstream system that consumes it
Because master data is always stored in a slower database
Because master data has no owner by definition
Because reports are never checked for accuracy at all
questions.explain: A wrong value in master data isn't contained to one place — it's distributed to every consuming system (CRM, billing, support, marketing), so one error becomes many.

questions.q: What is the difference between what matching (Chapter 2) solves and what data quality asks, per this lesson?
options: Matching answers how many records exist for an entity; quality asks whether the one surviving record is actually good
They are exactly the same question with different names
Matching is about product data only; quality is about customer data only
Quality only applies to reference data, never to master data
questions.explain: A record can be perfectly deduplicated to one golden record and still fail on completeness, accuracy, or validity — matching and quality are separate problems.

questions.q: A U.S. state code value that falls outside the defined two-letter code list fails which data quality dimension?
options: Validity
Timeliness
Uniqueness
Completeness
questions.explain: Validity is whether a populated value conforms to its defined format or domain — a code list membership check is a validity rule.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what four things does a master data quality scorecard typically track?
options: Percent complete, percent valid, duplicate rate, and staleness
Server uptime, CPU usage, disk space, and network latency
Number of employees, revenue, profit margin, and stock price
Font choice, color scheme, logo placement, and page layout
questions.explain: These four metrics turn the quality dimensions into trackable numbers over time, ideally tied to a named owner when they slip.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that 'fix at the source' beats cleansing rules inside the MDM hub?
options: Because a source system with no entry validation will keep generating bad records forever, no matter how much cleanup the hub does
Because cleansing rules inside the hub are illegal in most jurisdictions
Because source systems never produce any data quality problems
Because the hub cannot technically run any validation logic
questions.explain: Hub-side cleansing is a safety net, not a strategy — the durable fix is pushing validation back to the point of capture so bad data stops being created in the first place.
